passages.original: Me vero procul ab urbibus, foro, litibus, turbis remotum, sic quo pie (ut Quintilianus ait) latentem invenit invidia. Unde lectorem obsecro.
passages.english: But as for me, though I was far removed from cities, the forum, lawsuits and crowds, envy found me even so, hidden as I was (as Quintilian says). Therefore I implore the reader.
passages.notes: "sic quo pie" appears corrupt; the sense is presumably "even so" (perhaps for "sic quoque"), and it is translated that way. The sentence "Unde lectorem obsecro" breaks off without saying what the reader is implored to do.

passages.original: 305 (Cap. I. — Vers. 1.) « In principio fecit Deus coelum et terram. » Plerique existimant, sicut in altercatione 1 quoque Jasonis et Papisci scri- ptum est, et Tertullianus in libro contra Praxeam2 disputat : necnon Hilarius in expositione cujusnam Psalmi affirmat, in Hebreo-haberi : « In filio fecit Deus coelum et terram : » quod falsum esse ipsius rei veritas comprobat. Nam et Se- ptuaginta interpretes, et Symmachus, et Theo- dotion, in principio, transtulerunt.
passages.english: (Chapter 1, verse 1.) "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." Most people think, as is also written in the Dispute of Jason and Papiscus, and as Tertullian argues in his book Against Praxeas, and as Hilary too asserts in his exposition of one of the Psalms, that the Hebrew reads: "In the Son God made heaven and earth." The truth of the matter itself proves this false. For the Seventy translators, Symmachus and Theodotion all translated [it] "in the beginning."
passages.notes: The numbers "305", "1" and "2" are page and footnote marks and are omitted. "cujusnam Psalmi" is taken as "of some Psalm".

passages.original: (Vere. 13.) « Et elevavit Abrabam oculos suos : et ecce aries post tergum ejus tenebatur in virgulto Sabech cornibus suis. » Ridiculam rem in hoc loco Emisenus Eusebius est locutus : Sabech, inquiens, dicitur hircus, qui rectis cornibus et ad carpendas arboris frondes sublimis attollitur. Rursum Aquila συχνεώνα6, interpretatus est, quem nos veprem possumus dicere, vel spinetum : et ut verbi vim interpretemur, condensa et inter se implexa vir- gulta.
passages.english: (Verse 13.) "And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and behold, a ram behind his back was caught by its horns in the thicket Sabech." Eusebius of Emesa said something ridiculous on this passage. Sabech, he says, is the name of a he-goat that rears itself up high, with horns erect, to crop the leaves of a tree. Aquila, on the other hand, translated [it] as sychneōn, which we can call a bramble-bush or a thorn-thicket. To render the force of the word, [it means] dense and intertwined thickets.
passages.notes: "Vere." is read as "Vers." and "Abrabam" as "Abraham". The "6" after συχνεώνα is a footnote mark and is left out. Aquila's Greek term is given in transliteration.
